direct_answer: Diabetes can reduce feeling and blood flow in the feet, while arthritis and frailty can make it hard to reach and check them. Daily foot checks, well-fitting shoes, professional nail care and an annual diabetic foot check help prevent problems. New wounds or colour changes need prompt attention.

content:
Many people live with diabetes and arthritis together. Feet are where these conditions often meet.

This guide explains how to look after your feet and when to get help. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Why feet are at risk

  • Diabetes can cause nerve damage, so injuries may not be felt.
  • Reduced blood flow slows healing.
  • Arthritis can change foot shape and make reaching feet hard.
  • Frailty and poor balance increase falls risk.

Daily foot care

  • Check your feet daily, or ask someone to help. A mirror can help.
  • Look for cuts, blisters, redness, swelling or colour changes.
  • Wash and dry feet carefully, including between the toes.
  • Moisturise dry skin, but not between toes.

Nail care with diabetes

Cutting nails can be risky if you cannot see or reach your feet well. Ask about NHS podiatry, especially if you have been told your feet are at increased risk.

Footwear

Wear well-fitting shoes and check inside them for stones or rough areas. Avoid walking barefoot.

Regular checks

People with diabetes should have their feet checked at least once a year. NICE guidance sets out how foot risk is assessed.

When to get help

  • Call 999 if you are seriously unwell.
  • Get urgent help the same day from your GP, foot protection service or NHS 111 if you have a new wound, a foot that is hot, red, swollen or changing colour, or signs of infection.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

How often should my feet be checked?

At least yearly, and more often if you are at higher risk.

Can I cut my own nails?

Ask your diabetes team or podiatrist for advice.

Sources and further reading
